title: Views and Stored Procedures
description: Encapsulate complex queries as reusable views, and package business logic into parameterized stored procedures.

data.text: Database objects let you encapsulate logic so it lives in one place and is reused by every application that connects to SQL Server. Two of the most useful are **views** — saved queries you can query like tables — and **stored procedures** — parameterized T-SQL programs that execute on the server.

A view is a named SELECT statement. When you query the view, SQL Server expands it into the underlying query and runs it. Views are ideal for hiding complexity, enforcing consistent joins, or restricting which columns a user can see.

data.title: Creating a simple view
data.code:
CREATE VIEW sales.daily_sales
AS
SELECT
    YEAR(order_date)  AS y,
    MONTH(order_date) AS m,
    DAY(order_date)   AS d,
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    i.quantity * i.list_price AS sales
FROM   sales.orders AS o
INNER JOIN sales.order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
INNER JOIN production.products AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id;

data.text: Once created, query the view just like a table:

data.title: Querying a view

items: Simplify complex joins into a single queryable object
Restrict access — grant users SELECT on a view but not on the underlying table
Hide sensitive columns (e.g., exclude salary from a people view)
Provide a stable interface even if the underlying table schema changes

data.title: CREATE OR ALTER
data.text: Use CREATE OR ALTER (SQL Server 2016+) to update a view without dropping it first. This preserves permissions — DROP + CREATE would revoke them because the object is recreated.

A stored procedure is a precompiled block of T-SQL code that can accept parameters, execute one or more statements, and return results. Because the query plan is compiled once and reused, procedures are faster than ad-hoc queries.

data.title: Creating a stored procedure
Executing a stored procedure
OUTPUT parameters
data.text: Stored procedures can return data through SELECT result sets or through OUTPUT parameters (declared with OUTPUT in the parameter list). OUTPUT params are useful for returning scalar values like a calculated count or status code.

items: Always prefix with a schema (Sales.GetTopProducts, not just GetTopProducts) to avoid the dbo fallback and improve clarity
Use parameters, not string concatenation, for dynamic values — this prevents SQL injection
Keep procedures short and focused on one task — split complex logic into multiple procedures
Handle errors with TRY...CATCH and return meaningful status codes

data.title: Views and stored procedures
points: A view is a saved SELECT — query it like a table but it always reflects current data
CREATE OR ALTER updates a view or procedure without breaking permissions
Views are great for simplifying joins, hiding columns, and controlling access
Stored procedures accept parameters and reuse compiled query plans for speed
Use TRY...CATCH and schema-prefixed names for robust, maintainable procedures
